title: The Trial and Death of Socrates
author: Plato (translated by various translators)
publication_date: circa 399 BCE (original dialogues); various modern publication dates for translations
edition_analyzed: Standard complete edition containing Euthyphro, Apology, Crito, and Phaedo
target_audience: Readers interested in ethics, justice, and the foundations of Western thought
Anyone seeking to understand the Socratic method and the figure of Socrates
General readers interested in influential historical texts
core_themes: The nature of justice and law
Moral integrity and the examined life
Duty to the state versus personal conscience
The immortality of the soul and meaning of death
Civil disobedience and allegiance to truth
primary_purpose: To present and explore Socrates' philosophical teachings, his trial for impiety and corrupting the youth, his defense and ultimate acceptance of death, and to provoke thought about ethics, civic duty, and the value of philosophical inquiry.

structure_format.organization: Four linked dialogues—Euthyphro (the nature of piety), Apology (Socrates' defense speech), Crito (discussion of justice and legal obedience), Phaedo (discussion on the soul and afterlife)

key_concepts_lessons: Knowledge begins with acknowledgment of ignorance (Socratic wisdom).
One should not act unjustly, even when wronged.
It is better to suffer injustice than to commit it.
Law and morality are deeply interconnected, but conscience can override civic duty.
The soul's care and pursuit of virtue are paramount.
Death should not be feared by philosophers, as it may lead to greater wisdom or release from earthly concerns.
notable_features: Foundational source for Western philosophical thought
Origin of the Socratic method of questioning
Iconic examinations of law, ethics, and the meaning of life and death
Historical account of Socrates’ trial and death
cultural_historical_context: Written in the aftermath of Socrates' trial and execution in democratic Athens; these dialogues serve as both literary tributes and philosophical defenses of Socrates' teachings amid political turmoil, skepticism toward sophists, and debates over the nature of justice and piety.
reception_impact: Central text in philosophy, read and discussed worldwide for millennia
Profound influence on Western philosophy, ethics, politics, and education
Source of enduring questions about justice, civil disobedience, and the examined life
Regarded as essential reading in philosophy, classics, and law curricula
comparable_titles: Selected Dialogues by Plato (e.g., Republic, Symposium)
